analysis.one_liner: Bans stock, crypto, and derivatives trading by members of Congress, the president, Supreme Court justices, and Fed officials.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 5, 2025 and referred to four House committees the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has followed since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit members of Congress, the president, the vice president, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve bank presidents, and other top officials (and their spouses and dependent children) from holding or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and most cryptocurrencies. Officials would have to divest existing holdings within 120 days, face fines starting at 10% of the value of any violating holding, and the bill would require federal ethics offices to post all financial disclosure reports in searchable, downloadable online databases. It would also require officials to report when they or their businesses apply for or receive federal money such as contracts, grants, or loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans get a clearer view of officials' finances: all disclosure reports would be posted online in searchable form, and officials would have to report federal payments their households or businesses receive. The rules are also designed to reduce the risk that officials make decisions on issues where they personally hold stock — for example, defense or pharmaceutical legislation.

how_it_helps.text: Bars covered officials from holding or trading individual securities, futures, commodities, and most cryptocurrencies, and from holding net short positions [S2].
Requires divestiture of existing conflicting holdings within 120 days of enactment or of taking office, with limited extensions that must be posted publicly [S2].

Imposes a fine of at least 10% of the value of any financial interest held, bought, or sold in violation, and applies the ban even to interests held in trusts where the official is a beneficial owner [S2].

Requires the House, Senate, Office of Government Ethics, the courts, and the Federal Reserve to publish financial disclosure and transaction reports online in databases the public can search, sort, and download, with API access [S2].

Requires officials and their spouses and dependent children (including businesses they control) to report applications for or receipt of federal payments such as contracts, grants, and loans within 30 days, with a $5,000 fine for failing to report [S2].
Extends financial disclosure and trading rules to Federal Reserve bank presidents, vice presidents, and directors, who are not currently covered by the STOCK Act's regime [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent officials would bear the cost: they would have to sell individual stock holdings, give up a route to personal investment gains while in office, and disclose federal payments their families and businesses receive. Members of Congress, justices, and Fed officials would lose an investment option most Americans still have.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior officials

drawbacks.text: Enforcement depends on the same supervising ethics offices that police officials today; the bill replaces the existing criminal-penalty language for late transaction reports with a $1,000 civil fine per case [S2], and fines for trading violations are only meaningful if the offices actually impose them.

The ban is narrower than it first appears: diversified mutual funds, Treasury securities, and a spouse's primary-employer stock or compensation are all excluded [S2], so a well-advised official can keep substantial market exposure through funds — the main check is on individual stock picks.

Forced divestiture within 120 days can mean selling at whatever the market offers and paying transaction costs and, for some, capital gains taxes; officials may also shift to the excluded fund vehicles rather than truly exit the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: officials give up individual stock trading — something no law currently requires of them — in exchange for rules meant to remove the appearance and reality of officials trading on their own legislative and regulatory work. The bill's weaknesses are enforcement (fines and compliance left to ethics offices) and the fund exemption, which lets officials stay broadly invested. On balance, the transparency and conflict-of-interest gains outweigh the compliance costs, but the bill would be only as strong as the offices enforcing it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them has taken it up since, so it goes nowhere unless a committee schedules it.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Min (D-CA) introduced the bill on June 5, 2025 [S1].
The Speaker referred it to four committees — Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means — for portions within each committee's jurisdiction [S4].
The only recorded action since introduction is the committee referral; there is no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action in the record [S4].
All 18 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has joined [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As things stand, incumbent officeholders — members of Congress, senior executive officials, Supreme Court justices, and Federal Reserve bank officials — are better off: nothing has changed, so they keep their current ability to trade individual stocks and their current, harder-to-search disclosure regime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent officials who can still trade

for.name: Rep. Dave Min
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 5, 2025 and authored the trading ban, divestiture rules, and online disclosure requirements.

for.name: Nine original cosponsors (Reps. Norton, Ansari, Levin, Tlaib, Deluzio, Ramirez, Keating, Horsford, and Stanton)
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction on June 5, 2025.

for.name: 18 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; the bill has no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Chairs of the Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees
against.role: Committee chairs controlling whether the bill gets a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Have not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred on June 5, 2025; the record shows no committee action [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors are Democrats, and the Republican-run committees that received the bill have taken no action on it [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders (members of Congress, the president and vice president, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve officials)
industries.note: The bill would strip these officials of the ability to hold and trade individual stocks, futures, commodities, and most cryptocurrencies while in office and for 120 days after leaving, and would force them to disclose federal payments to their households and businesses. Their institutional interest in keeping the status quo runs against the transparency the bill would create.

industries.industry: Diversified mutual funds and index funds
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes diversified registered investment funds and Treasury securities from the trading ban, making them the compliant path for officials who want market exposure. That steers officials' money into the fund industry rather than away from investing altogether.

industries.industry: Federal Reserve banks and their officers
industries.note: Fed bank presidents, vice presidents, and directors would be brought under financial disclosure rules and the trading ban for the first time, supervised by the Fed's Inspector General. Their regional bank institutions lose discretion their officers currently have over their own investment activity.

analysis.trajectory: With a four-committee referral, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action for the rest of 2025, the bill is on the path most stock-trading-ban proposals have taken: it will likely sit without a hearing unless leadership decides to prioritize it. If it is not taken up before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, it dies and would have to be reintroduced.
